title: EPA Rescinds 2009 Greenhouse-Gas Endangerment Finding and Vehicle GHG Standards
description_short: EPA Rescinds 2009 Greenhouse-Gas Endangerment Finding and Vehicle GHG Standards
description_medium: EPA finalized a rule on February 12, 2026 rescinding the 2009 greenhouse-gas Endangerment Finding and repealing federal greenhouse-gas emission standards for on-road motor vehicles and engines that relied on that finding. EPA described the action as its largest deregulatory action. The stored future-emissions totals should be omitted unless separately sourced to a transparent analysis.
description_long: On February 12, 2026, the Environmental Protection Agency finalized a rule rescinding its 2009 Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding and repealing later greenhouse-gas emission standards for light-, medium-, and heavy-duty highway vehicles and engines that relied on that finding. EPA said that without the finding it lacked authority under Section 202(a) of the Clean Air Act to prescribe those standards. The agency stated that the final action applied to greenhouse-gas requirements and did not change rules for traditional air pollutants. EPA also said manufacturers would no longer have future obligations to measure, control, and report greenhouse-gas emissions for covered highway vehicles and engines. Those descriptions reflect the agency’s stated rule and rationale; the stored future-emissions estimates are not included because the supplied record says they lack a transparent supporting analysis. The entry records the finalized regulatory action, rather than a projection of its eventual climate effects or the outcome of any legal challenge.

title: 2025 Reconciliation Law Delays Provisions in Two Medicaid Eligibility Rules
description_short: 2025 Reconciliation Law Delays Provisions in Two Medicaid Eligibility Rules
description_medium: The 2025 reconciliation law imposed a 10-year delay on specified provisions in two Biden-era Medicaid eligibility rules: the 2023 Medicare Savings Program rule and the 2024 Eligibility and Enrollment rule. KFF, citing CBO, reported that delaying the two rules together was projected to reduce federal spending by about $122 billion over 10 years and increase the uninsured population by about 400,000 in 2034. An earlier estimate that 1.3 million dual-eligible beneficiaries would lose Medicaid applied to the House-passed legislation and should not be presented as the final law's precise effect.
description_long: The 2025 reconciliation law delayed until October 2034 parts of two Biden-era Medicaid and CHIP eligibility rules: the 2023 Medicare Savings Program rule and the 2024 Eligibility and Enrollment rule. The rules were intended to reduce administrative barriers to enrolling in and keeping coverage. KFF, citing Congressional Budget Office estimates, reported that delaying provisions in both rules would reduce federal spending by about $122 billion over 10 years and increase the uninsured population by roughly 400,000 in 2034. That estimate differs from an earlier 1.3 million figure for dual-eligible beneficiaries, which applied to the House-passed bill rather than the final law. The distinction matters because the legislation changed during negotiations and estimates tied to earlier versions should not be presented as final effects. The projected coverage changes are not counts of people already losing insurance; they describe a modeled future impact if the delayed rules do not take effect. The law’s delay may affect access and renewal processes for low-income beneficiaries.

title: MAGA Inc. Invitation Lists $1 Million per Person for Trump-Featured Mar-a-Lago Dinner
description_short: MAGA Inc. invitation listed a $1 million per-person price for a Trump-featured dinner
description_medium: WIRED reproduced an invitation for MAGA Inc.’s March 1, 2025 candlelight dinner at Mar-a-Lago featuring President Trump; it listed a price of $1 million per person. Axios separately reported that MAGA Inc. sought as much as $1 million per seat for Trump-featured fundraisers. The reports establish an advertised price, not that a named guest paid or pitched a cryptocurrency project.
description_long: MAGA Inc., a pro-Trump super PAC, invited donors to a March 1, 2025 candlelight dinner at Mar-a-Lago featuring President Donald Trump. WIRED reported that the invitation it reviewed listed a price of $1 million per person to reserve a seat. Axios separately reported that MAGA Inc. was charging as much as $1 million per plate for fundraisers featuring Trump. These reports support describing a high advertised price for political fundraising access. They do not establish that every invitee attended or paid the listed amount. The supplied reporting also does not substantiate the original claim that crypto entrepreneur Ari Schiermeyer paid $1 million at this dinner or pitched Trump on a token project. A high seat price alone does not prove an exchange for official action. The corrected entry is limited to the invitation and reported fundraising price; individual payments, conversations, and any policy benefit would require separate records or reporting.

title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia returned to U.S. after mistaken deportation to El Salvador
description_short: Kilmar Abrego Garcia returned to U.S. after mistaken deportation to El Salvador
description_medium: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whom the Trump administration had mistakenly deported to El Salvador despite an order barring his removal there, was returned to the United States on June 6, 2025 to face federal migrant-smuggling charges. By late June and July he was in federal custody in Tennessee while litigation continued over his detention, prosecution and the administration's earlier compliance with the court order. The July entry saying he remained in an El Salvador prison is incorrect.
description_long: Kilmar Abrego Garcia was returned to the United States on June 6, 2025, after the Trump administration mistakenly deported him to El Salvador despite an order barring his removal there. He came back to face federal migrant-smuggling charges and was held in federal custody in Tennessee by late June, as litigation continued over his detention and prosecution. That chronology corrects the later July claim that he was still imprisoned in El Salvador. The return did not resolve the separate dispute over how the administration handled the original removal order or the legal basis for his continued detention. The supplied reporting records the return and a subsequent court appearance concerning bail conditions; it does not establish the outcome of every related case. Keeping these events distinct avoids treating his return as either a full remedy for the mistaken deportation or proof that all court directives had been satisfied. The case drew national attention to the administration’s compliance with judicial orders in immigration matters and to the consequences for a person wrongly sent abroad. This entry focuses on the verified sequence and the unresolved litigation rather than repeating the inaccurate location claim.

title: Trump Signs Order Directing Pentagon Policy Restricting Transgender Military Service
description_short: Trump’s January 2025 order directed a new policy restricting transgender military service
description_medium: On January 27, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14183, which directed the Defense Department to implement a policy restricting transgender military service and revoked the prior administration’s policy. DoD issued implementation guidance in February. A March 18 court opinion records an injunction blocking enforcement at that stage. The order was not signed on inauguration day and did not itself discharge every service member.
description_long: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14183, “Prioritizing Military Excellence and Readiness,” on January 27, 2025. The order revoked prior policy and directed the Defense Department to treat gender dysphoria as inconsistent with the administration’s standard for military service, with DoD implementation to follow. The department issued implementation guidance on February 26. In a March 18 opinion, a federal district court described the order and implementation policy and blocked enforcement at that stage of the litigation. The signing date was not January 20, and the order itself did not immediately discharge every transgender service member. The supplied order and opinion do not establish the number of affected personnel, the status of every individual separation, or the final outcome of the legal challenges. This account distinguishes the presidential directive, later department guidance, and the court’s temporary intervention. It does not present the policy as continuously enforceable or claim a final ruling beyond the cited record.

title: Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts Files Chapter 11 Petitions in November 2004
description_short: Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts and subsidiaries filed Chapter 11 petitions on November 21, 2004
description_medium: Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts, Inc. and certain subsidiaries filed voluntary Chapter 11 petitions in New Jersey on November 21, 2004, according to the company’s SEC Form 10-K. The filing followed an October 20 restructuring support agreement. The SEC filing identifies the corporate debtors and does not establish a broad count such as “the fourth Trump bankruptcy.”
description_long: Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts, Inc. and certain subsidiaries filed voluntary Chapter 11 petitions in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of New Jersey on November 21, 2004, according to the company’s SEC Form 10-K. The filing described a prearranged reorganization; a restructuring support agreement among the debtors, Donald Trump, and noteholders was dated October 20. That agreement date is not the court petition date. The company reported approximately $1.8 billion in public indebtedness. The proceeding concerned the named corporate debtors, not a personal bankruptcy by Trump. The supplied 10-K supports this company’s filing and date but does not establish that it was the “fourth Trump bankruptcy” across all associated entities. The entry records the Chapter 11 filing and its chronology without making a broader count or inferring creditor recoveries from the debt total. The SEC filing does not describe creditors’ later recoveries or the reorganization’s ultimate results.

title: Trump Removes Office of Special Counsel Head Hampton Dellinger
description_short: Trump Fires Office of Special Counsel Head Hampton Dellinger
description_medium: The Supreme Court’s order records that Hampton Dellinger was removed as head of the Office of Special Counsel on February 7, 2025, and that a district court temporarily reinstated him during litigation. The order documents procedural relief, not abolition of the office, termination of its statutory functions, or a final ruling on the removal’s legality.
description_long: The Supreme Court’s order in the emergency proceedings records that Hampton Dellinger was removed as head of the Office of Special Counsel on February 7, 2025, and that a district court temporarily reinstated him while litigation proceeded. The case concerned the removal of an agency head and temporary judicial relief during the dispute. The order does not say that the Office of Special Counsel was abolished or that its whistleblower and Hatch Act responsibilities ended. It also does not establish a final merits ruling on the president’s authority to remove Dellinger. The original January 20 date is not supported by the cited order. This entry is limited to the documented removal and temporary reinstatement, which are distinct procedural events. It does not infer that the office stopped operating, describe downstream enforcement effects, or treat an emergency order as a final resolution of the underlying case. Later decisions or agency records would be needed to describe the ultimate legal outcome.
